<reason>Side B (PRO) won by anchoring to the motion's actual text — "bear more legal responsibility," not "fault" — and showing that A's own constructive program (mandatory fare-funded injury surcharge, verified ID, app-deducted fines, suspensions, penalties for missed slowdowns) is exactly that, leaving A defending a semantic wall between "funding rules" and "responsibility." That wall eroded because the fund pays victims directly from company revenue, and because A drifted from "no wrongful act" to conceding the omitted slowdown is "the company's own breach," which B's closing exploited to revive concurrent causation in the geofenced-plaza cases the motion explicitly covers. A landed real hits: the GPS-margin dilemma forced B to confine its presumption to provable zones, and the funding-vs-fault distinction was pressed with discipline and clean format compliance. But B answered both pressure dilemmas directly (four-tools-not-one; pay-first-then-recover via familiar no-fault structures), and A's case ultimately converged with the motion's plain wording — "only one side is arguing the motion says so." B's two clipped rebuttals are a genuine execution cost, holding the margin to clear-but-competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 seizure of A's surcharge concession — "A legal obligation, imposed on the company, to fund pedestrian injuries its riders cause. That is the motion." — reframed the entire debate; A spent three speeches arguing a label and never escaped the capture, since the motion says "legal responsibility," not "fault."</best_rebuttal>
